item.title: Don’t blame just SpaceX for the launch capacity crunch
item.description: Perhaps the biggest topic of discussion in the space industry in the last few months involves the future of the Falcon 9. That discourse has evolved from SpaceX ending its popular rideshare launch program to halting commercial sales of the rocket entirely and, potentially, winding down launches for the U.S. government. What has become arguably the world’s most successful rocket may soon retire.

item.title: Protection or preparation for attack? Counterspace capabilities, international law and nuclear command and control
item.description: Space militarization is not new, but its pace and breadth have increased sharply. The Secure World Foundation’s 2026 assessment documents counterspace capabilities being developed by 13 countries across five categories as of Feb. 28: co-orbital systems, direct-ascent weapons, electronic warfare, directed energy and cyber operations. The report finds that only non-destructive counterspace capabilities were being used in active military conflicts at that point.

item.title: Why the space sector needs to take a project-centric approach to strategy
item.description: Throughout my career, I have seen organizations develop bold strategies, pursue high risk missions and deliver ambitious goals. But in my experience, the difference between strategic success and failure rarely comes down to the vision itself. So why are some strategies delivered successfully, while others fail to achieve their goals?

item.title: Eighteen launches, no program names: a call for disclosure
item.description: On the evening of October 15, a Falcon 9 lifted off from Space Launch Complex 4 East at Vandenberg carrying a classified payload for the Space Force. The booster, B1081, came back to the droneship on its 28th flight. SpaceX ended the broadcast at stage separation, as it does. The payload was not described, the satellites were not counted and no program was named.

item.title: Space is a warfighting domain. Our industrial base must reflect that.
item.description: When I served as acting Secretary of Defense, I took a trip to Buckley Space Force Base. I went as someone who understood in the abstract that space had become contested. I left understanding it in my gut. Watching the men and women who track every object on orbit and leverage space-based sensors to spot a launch anywhere on Earth to give our ground forces the seconds of warning that save lives, I came away with a conviction that has only deepened since: Space is a warfighting domain, and we are not yet organized to win in it.
